question: What is required to deliver a prefabricated timber facade with non-repeating panels within a Minergie envelope?

answer.answer:
Prefabrication (PR2) is the process you have to stand up, and everything the literature cites as its requirement is organisational rather than mechanical: early contractor involvement (CO11), DfMA for DFAB process (PR9) and an integrated supply chain (VA14) upstream of it, with precise planning (RI14) and regulatory/legal concern (RI18) as the two things it depends on, and no machine among them. Non-repeating panels are delivered through a configurator/kit-of-parts (AR6) feeding mass-customisation (PR11), which in turn rests on highly standardised (AT7) component coordination, so the variety is bought with standardisation underneath, not instead of it. Bespoke/customised design (AT1) constrains modularity (AT2) on a path carried by only 4 of the 50 cases, and the watch item on the other side is design compromise/over standardised (RI15), drawn on by 17. What the off-site route returns is schedule (VA2), quality (VA3), fewer errors (VA10) and site safety (VA13); the record names no energy-performance standard, so envelope certification falls under the general regulatory concern.

**What prefabrication itself requires.** PR2's edge set is complete in the context, so these counts are totals. Three enablers are cited as making prefabrication possible: early contractor involvement enables prefabrication/off-site, on peer-reviewed evidence, carried by 13 of the 50 coded cases, because integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party to be involved in the early design phase [1]; DfMA for DFAB process enables prefabrication/off-site, carried by 15 of the 50, orienting the project toward offsite manufacture [1]; and integrate supply chain enables prefabrication/off-site, carried by 12 of the 50 [1]. Two further edges run the other way, as dependencies of PR2: prefabrication depends on rely on precise planning, carried by 18 of the 50, because it relies on precise up-front planning and logistics [1], and prefabrication depends on regulatory/legal concern, carried by 10 of the 50, since a functional regulatory system for offsite compliance requires third-party certification and traceability [1]. That last edge is the nearest thing in front of me to an envelope-certification requirement. Categorically, CO11 is a Condition, PR9 a Process, VA14 a Value, RI14 and RI18 Risks: none is a Resource, so the cited preconditions for going off-site are about who is in the room, how the design is structured and what can be proved, not about equipment.

The counts are uneven in their own right: rely on precise planning is drawn on by 36 of the 50 coded cases [1], against 14 for early contractor involvement [1], 15 for DfMA for DFAB process [1] and 14 for integrate supply chain [1], with prefabrication/off-site itself drawn on by 20 [1].

**Getting non-repeating panels out of an off-site line.** The cited path runs from highly standardised to configurators/kit-of-parts, on standards evidence, carried by 11 of the 50, since modular coordination permits the interchangeability of different components [1], and then from configurators/kit-of-parts to mass-customisation, peer-reviewed, carried by 9 of the 50, the configurator integrating customisation data into robotic manufacturing [1]. Configurators/kit-of-parts is drawn on by 12 of the 50 [1] and mass-customisation by 17 [1], while highly standardised is drawn on by 25 [1]. The counter-pressure is explicit: bespoke/customised design constrains modular, peer-reviewed and carried by 4 of the 50, because integral architecture couples functions tightly to components and so constrains modular interchange [1]. Bespoke/customised design is drawn on by 10 of the 50 [1], modular by 12 [1], and design compromise/over standardised by 17, an edgeless Risk in the cited layer, so the evidence for it is the case count and co-occurrence rather than any asserted mechanism [1]. Highly standardised also enables reduce construction complexity, on standards evidence, carried by 15 of the 50, the base module standard reducing component variety and coordinating design, manufacture and assembly [1].

If the panels are to be set robotically, note the direction: robotic assembly has prefabrication/off-site as a precondition, carried by 4 of the 50, since automated delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [1]. Prefabrication is upstream of the robot, not a consequence of it.

**What it returns.** Prefabrication enables reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency, carried by 19 of the 50 [1], improve quality/performance, carried by 18, through the controlled factory environment [1], reduce errors/constraints, carried by 14 [1], and improve site safety, carried by 12, by moving work offsite [1]. On PR2's own outbound set, the schedule and quality returns are the most widely carried and safety the least, though improve site safety is drawn on by 39 of the 50 cases overall [1], mostly by routes other than this one.

**Deployed record.** Timber facade work at scale is present: census_RXH10-2 performs assembly and timber joinery cutting on the structural core and the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, at technology readiness level 9 [2], and it uses timber [3]; the context gives no firm for it. Off-site timber lines of the kind a facade panel plant would sit in are recorded as RP3, which performs assembly and timber joinery cutting on the structural core, deployed off-site, at technology readiness level 9 [4], RP6, adopted to address digital, likewise assembly and timber joinery cutting, off-site, at technology readiness level 9 [5] and RP7, adopted to address digital and market, on the same work off-site at technology readiness level 9 [6]. Two timber records carry named developers: census_RXT1-2, developed by Firm_128, in timber [7], and census_RXT9-1, developed by Firm_171, also timber [8], though the context gives no process profile for either. On the facade side but off the timber path, RP8 performs inspection and material handling on the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, deployed off-site, at technology readiness level 9 [9]. The context does not say which enablers any of these cases draw on, so I cannot tell you that a given deployment exhibits the configurator route or the DfMA route; the case-level and enabler-level evidence here sit side by side rather than joined.

**Limits.** The energy standard you name does not appear in the retrieved material, so I cannot say what the record holds about envelope certification beyond the regulatory/legal dependency of prefabrication. The co-occurrence figures listed here are statistical association, not asserted dependency, and the cited dependency layer is thin by design: 100 edges touch 68 of the 140 enablers, leaving 72 with no cited edge, which is a property of the literature and not of the record [1].

**Deployed evidence.** Selected by filtering the coded records, not by similarity. 6 records in the graph carry timber as their material; all are listed below. 27 records in the graph carry Envelope/Facade as their building system; all are listed below. Showing the first 15 of 33, so this listing is a cut of the filtered set, though the counts above are exact.
- RP3, adopted to address quality, integration, market; performs assembly, timber joinery cutting; works on the structural core; deployed off-site; at technology readiness level 9.

- RP22, adopted to address cost, market; performs 3d printing, assembly, material handling; works on sitework, the building envelope, the facade, or curtain wall; deployed as a mobile robot, off-site, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 7.
- RP29, adopted to address quality, safety, labor, market; performs assembly, tiling; works on the building envelope, the facade, or curtain wall; at technology readiness level 9.
